title: Context Harvest: conference debrief and experiment sketch
content:
Quick debrief notes from Context & Inference workshop (collected during talks + hallway convos). Informal — brain dump for sprint planning.

Topline takeaways:
- Practical KV/cache tricks matter more than marginal model gains for long contexts — both latency and token-cost win.
- Prefetch + staged eviction beats naive LRU on mixed session lengths (talk: Z. Alvarez). Worth prototyping for our streaming use cases.
- Compression-in-cache: small lossy transforms (quantized deltas, hash anchors) gave 2x cache capacity with ~0.5% utility drop in demos.
- Multi-granularity indexing (sentence-level + chunk-level) reduces misses for conversational apps where relevant spans are small.

Notes to self:
- Revisit current KV layout: we store token-level keys per layer; can we add a secondary sentence-hash index at write time? cheap to compute.
- Experiment idea A: "two-tier cache". Keep recent token-kv for first N tokens; maintain a separate compressed chunk index for older context. Evict policy: prefer dropping compressed chunks first. Hypothesis: preserves immediate latency while increasing effective context coverage.
- Experiment idea B: On-the-fly chunk consolidation. Background job that compacts small nearby chunks into a single compressed entry when GPU load < 30%.

Short implementation sketch (notes, not final):
- Add index table: sentence_hash -> (item_id, byte_range) stored in Redis (or Rocks for private).
- Compression format: 8-bit uniform quant + simple delta + zstd; benchmarks needed.
- API change: include preferred_recall_window param in request to bias routing to compressed-hits. Keep default unchanged for backwards compat.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Cost model: how does added CPU (compression/decompression) and extra Redis look vs token cost saved on GPU? Need microbenchmarks with our deduped token billing.
- Quality: how to detect when compression causes semantic drift? cheap probe: run a small QA arbiter on compressed reconstruction (10 qps sample).
- Consistency across model variants: some quantized runtime variants may not support layer-wise kv reconstruction. Fallback planning needed.

Actionable next steps (for 1-week spike):
1) Prototype two-tier cache locally (Ravi) — naive in-memory implementation with toggles. Metric: hit-rate, tail-latency, CPU overhead.
2) Compression baseline (Mina) — implement a tiny pipeline: float->8bit->zstd and measure decode time on CPU and GPU-friendly paths.
3) Cost calc (me) — run toy workload using our billing table to estimate per-request savings vs infra cost.
4) Quick eval harness: pick 3 product prompts (chat, summarization, retrieval-augmented) and measure end-to-end quality delta when older context replaced by compressed chunks.

Meeting notes / quotes that stuck:
- "Cache is a model of the user, not of the model." — good framing for prioritization.
- "Evictions are policy, not destiny" — try optimistic retention for high-value tokens.

Links mentioned in talks I want to read properly later:
- paper: "Compressed KV Stores for Long Contexts" (preprint, 2026) — pdf link scribbled on napkin, add to reading list.
- repo: demo of staged-evict (internal prototype) — asked for access from author in Slack.

TODO (personal):
- Add a simple chart in Confluence comparing our current hit-rate curve vs hypothesized two-tier approach.
- Draft a short 1-pager for product: why this matters for retail chat and note-taking (focus on cost + user retention).

Misc scribbles:
- If decode cost too high on CPU, consider delegating decompress to tiny GPU kernel or do partial decompress only for top-k retrieval.
- Consider making compression deterministic to improve deduping across sessions.

End of dump — keep this light. Will turn into proper README + spike tickets after initial experiments.
